Step by Step Instructions for someone selling a Vehicle privately through Facebook Marketplace in Ontario - For someone that has never sold a vehicle privately?

ChatGPT said:

Absolutely. For a first-time private seller in Ontario, the process is actually fairly straightforward once you separate it into three parts:

  1. Prepare the vehicle and listing

  2. Complete the sale safely

  3. Complete the Ontario ownership paperwork correctly

The biggest mistakes are usually around the UVIP, the vehicle permit, licence plates, payment, and letting the buyer drive away without proper insurance/registration.

Step-by-step: Selling a Vehicle Privately Through Facebook Marketplace in Ontario

Phase 1 — Get the vehicle ready to sell

Step 1: Decide whether you are selling it "as-is" or with a Safety Standards Certificate

You have two basic approaches.

Option A — Sell it without a Safety Standards Certificate

This is often the simplest approach for an older/high-kilometre vehicle.

You advertise it honestly as something like:

"Sold as-is. Safety Standards Certificate not included."

The buyer can purchase it and then arrange the safety inspection themselves.

A Safety Standards Certificate (SSC) is not a warranty; it only confirms that the vehicle met Ontario's minimum safety standards at the time of inspection. Ontario

Option B — Get it safetied before selling

You take it to a licensed DriveON inspection facility, pay for the inspection/repairs, and obtain the certificate if it passes.

This can make the vehicle more attractive to buyers because the buyer knows it has passed the safety inspection.

An SSC is valid for 36 calendar days from the inspection. Ontario

For an older, high-mileage car, I'd generally avoid spending a large amount repairing it solely to obtain a safety certificate unless the resulting increase in selling price is likely to justify it.

Phase 2 — Get your Ontario paperwork ready

Step 2: Find your vehicle ownership permit

You need the Ontario Vehicle Permit — commonly called the "green ownership."

Check that:

  • Your name is on it.

  • The VIN matches the VIN physically displayed on the vehicle.

  • The vehicle information is correct.

Ontario specifically says sellers should verify that the VIN on the vehicle matches the VIN on the permit before selling. Ontario

Do not give the buyer the entire permit without completing the transfer section.

The permit has two important portions:

Vehicle portion → goes to the buyer after you complete the transfer.

Plate portion → you keep.

Ontario uses a plate-to-owner system, meaning the plates belong to you rather than the vehicle. Ontario+1

Step 3: Check whether there is a lien on the vehicle

Before advertising the car, determine whether money is still owing against it.

For example, this can happen if you financed the vehicle and the financing company registered a lien.

Your UVIP will contain lien information. Ontario specifically recommends checking the lien/debt information before selling. Ontario

If there is an outstanding lien, don't simply tell the buyer "I'll pay it off after you give me the money."

Deal with the lender and obtain appropriate documentation showing the lien has been discharged.

This is particularly important because a lien can follow the vehicle.

Step 4: Buy a Used Vehicle Information Package (UVIP)

This is one of the most important steps.

For a normal private sale of a used car in Ontario, the seller is legally required to provide the buyer with a UVIP. Ontario+1

The UVIP contains things such as:

  • Vehicle identification information

  • Ontario registration history

  • Previous/current owner information

  • Recorded odometer information

  • Lien information

  • Registration status

  • Certain vehicle-history information

  • Ontario wholesale-value/tax information

  • Bill of Sale section

The current government cost is $20. Ontario

You can obtain it online or at a ServiceOntario location.

Important:

Get the UVIP before you finalize the sale.

Don't rely on the buyer saying:

"I'll just get one myself."

The legal responsibility to provide it rests with the seller. Ontario

Step 5: Review the UVIP yourself

When you receive it, check that everything makes sense.

Pay particular attention to:

VIN

Compare the UVIP → ownership → VIN on the vehicle.

Registration history

Make sure the ownership history isn't surprising.

Lien information

Make sure you know whether there is outstanding financing.

Vehicle status

Look for things such as rebuilt/wrecked status or other information that could affect the sale.

Ontario specifically recommends checking the VIN and looking for discrepancies in vehicle-history information. Ontario+1

Phase 3 — Prepare the Facebook Marketplace listing

Step 6: Photograph the vehicle thoroughly

For a private sale, I'd take more photographs than you think you need.

At minimum:

  • Front

  • Rear

  • Both sides

  • Four corners

  • Hood

  • Roof

  • Wheels/tires

  • Interior

  • Dashboard with engine running

  • Odometer

  • Engine bay

  • Trunk

  • VIN plate/sticker, but I generally wouldn't publicly display the complete VIN in the Marketplace advertisement

  • Any damage

  • Scratches/dents

  • Tire wear

  • Warning lights

The objective is to make the buyer feel that you're not hiding anything.

Step 7: Be extremely honest about condition

This is especially important with an older vehicle.

Don't write:

"Runs great!"

when there are known problems.

Instead:

"Vehicle starts, runs and drives. Air conditioning works. Check-engine light is not illuminated. There is some cosmetic damage to the rear bumper and the driver's seat has wear."

A private sale doesn't mean you can deliberately misrepresent material information.

Being upfront also reduces the likelihood of arguments after the sale.

Step 8: State the important numbers

Your listing should clearly provide:

Year:
Make:
Model:
Trim:
Mileage:
Transmission:
Engine:
Drive type:
Safety certificate: Yes/No
Accident history: if known
Lien status: No lien / explain situation
Location:
Price:

And clearly indicate:

Private sale — not a dealership.

Phase 4 — Communicating with Facebook buyers

Step 9: Expect scammers

Marketplace vehicle sales attract scams.

Be suspicious of:

"I'm out of town but I'll send my cousin."

"I'll send you a certified cheque."

"I'll pay you through PayPal."

"I'll send an e-transfer but you need to refund the excess."

"I'll send a courier."

"I need your email to arrange payment."

"Can you buy a CARFAX for me from this particular website?"

The safest transaction is generally:

Buyer physically meets you → examines vehicle → agrees to purchase → payment is independently verified → paperwork is completed → vehicle is handed over.

Step 10: Don't give the buyer the car for an extended "test drive"

For a private sale, you don't want a stranger disappearing down the highway with your car.

Before allowing a test drive:

  • See their driver's licence.

  • Confirm they are properly licensed to drive.

  • Accompany them.

  • Keep the keys with you until you're ready for the test drive.

  • Don't let them take the vehicle alone.

You can also arrange the test drive around a mechanic if the buyer wants an inspection.

Ontario itself recommends that buyers inspect the vehicle and have a trusted mechanic inspect it. Ontario+1

Phase 5 — The buyer wants to buy it

This is where you want to slow down.

Don't just hand over the keys because someone says:

"I'll take it."

There are several things that should happen in a particular order.

Step 11: Agree on the final price

For example:

"We've agreed on $4,500."

Make sure both parties understand:

  • Exact purchase price

  • Whether the vehicle is being sold as-is

  • Whether an SSC is included

  • What accessories are included

  • Whether there are any known problems

Don't leave these things ambiguous.

Step 12: Complete the Bill of Sale

Ontario requires the Bill of Sale to contain specific information.

It must include things such as:

  • VIN

  • Make

  • Year

  • Power source

  • Body type

  • Colour

  • Model, where available

  • Purchase price

  • Seller's name/address/signature

  • Buyer's name/address

  • Date of sale

Ontario allows the Bill of Sale to be handwritten or printed, and the UVIP contains a dedicated Bill of Sale section that you can use. Ontario

Best practice

I would make two copies:

Buyer gets: original.

Seller keeps: signed copy/photo/scan.

Have both parties sign and date it.

Step 13: Complete the transfer section on your vehicle permit

This is extremely important.

On the back of the vehicle permit is the Application for Transfer.

You, the current owner, complete and sign the seller portion and provide it to the buyer.

Ontario's Highway Traffic Act specifically requires the seller, when ownership ends, to remove the plates, retain the plate portion of the permit, and complete/sign the transfer application on the vehicle portion given to the new owner. Ontario

Do not leave this blank for the buyer to fill out later.

Step 14: Give the buyer the documents

At the completion of the sale, the buyer should receive:

1. Vehicle portion of your ownership permit

With the transfer section completed/signed.

2. UVIP

Including the completed Bill of Sale section, or a separate Bill of Sale.

3. Safety Standards Certificate

Only if you obtained one/is applicable to your arrangement.

Ontario says the seller gives the buyer the UVIP, signed Bill of Sale and completed transfer application, and the safety certificate if required/being provided. Ontario

Step 15: Remove YOUR licence plates

This is absolutely critical.

The buyer does NOT get your plates.

Remove the front and rear plates before the vehicle leaves.

Ontario plates stay with the owner rather than the vehicle. Ontario+1

You keep:

The licence plates

and

The plate portion of the vehicle permit

You can use the plates on another vehicle in accordance with Ontario's registration rules, or return them to ServiceOntario if you no longer need them. Ontario+1

Step 16: Make sure payment is actually received

This may be the single biggest practical risk in a private sale.

For cash

Meet at a bank if possible.

Have the buyer withdraw/deposit the money at the bank.

You can then verify that everything is legitimate.

For e-transfer

Don't accept:

"Here's a screenshot showing that I sent it."

Verify that the money is actually in your account.

Don't release the vehicle based solely on an email or screenshot.

Also watch for fake/intercepted e-transfer notifications.

Bank draft/certified cheque

Be careful.

A legitimate-looking cheque isn't necessarily the same as confirmed cleared funds.

A bank meeting is much safer than accepting a cheque from a stranger and letting them drive away immediately.

Step 17: Only hand over the vehicle after payment and paperwork are complete

A good order is:

1. Buyer inspects vehicle

↓

2. Agree on price

↓

3. Payment is completed and verified

↓

4. Bill of Sale is signed

↓

5. Vehicle permit transfer is completed

↓

6. Buyer receives UVIP/documentation

↓

7. You remove your plates

↓

8. Buyer takes possession

This gives you a clear transaction record.

Phase 6 — What does the buyer do after leaving?

This is important because the buyer cannot simply drive the car away with your plates.

The buyer needs to arrange:

Insurance

and

Registration

before legally driving the vehicle on Ontario roads.

Ontario requires a buyer of a used vehicle to register it within 6 days of purchase. Ontario+1

The buyer will generally take the required documents to ServiceOntario, including the UVIP, Bill of Sale, vehicle permit, proof of insurance and, where required, the Safety Standards Certificate. Ontario

They will then receive their own registration/plate arrangement.

What if the buyer wants to drive it home?

This is something that should be discussed before the transaction.

The buyer cannot legally solve this by simply putting your plates back on the car after you've removed them.

Ontario has temporary/special permit options in certain circumstances. A temporary licence plate sticker can allow eligible vehicles to be driven for limited purposes such as going to a garage for a safety inspection. Ontario

The buyer should therefore arrange the appropriate insurance and temporary/permanent registration solution before taking the vehicle onto the road.

For an older vehicle being sold privately, another practical solution is for the buyer to arrange a tow/trailer.

Step 18: Notify your insurance company

Once the sale is completed, tell your insurer that you have sold the vehicle.

Give them:

  • Date of sale

  • Time of sale

  • VIN

  • Buyer information if requested

  • Confirmation that you no longer own the vehicle

Don't simply assume that because you've physically handed over the vehicle everything automatically happens with your insurer.

Step 19: Keep your records

I'd keep a complete digital folder containing:

Original/signed Bill of Sale

Copy/photo of UVIP

Photo of completed vehicle transfer

Photo of vehicle at time of sale

Copy of payment record

Marketplace listing

Marketplace messages

Buyer identification/contact information

Any mechanic inspection reports

Any disclosures you've made about known problems

I'd keep this for several years.

Step 20: Keep the licence plate portion of your permit

Don't accidentally give the buyer the part you need to retain.

Ontario specifically says the seller keeps the plate portion of the permit. Ontario

You'll need it if you later put those plates onto another vehicle.

A very simple "day of sale" checklist

Ontario Private Vehicle Sale — Day-of-Sale Checklist

Before the Buyer Arrives

  • Have the original Vehicle Permit/ownership.

  • Have the UVIP.

  • Review the UVIP and confirm the VIN matches the vehicle.

  • Have a Bill of Sale prepared.

  • Have a pen available.

  • Have your licence/identification available.

  • Have the vehicle reasonably clean.

  • Remove personal belongings.

  • Have all vehicle keys/remotes ready.

  • Decide in advance how payment will be verified.

  • Decide in advance whether the vehicle is being sold with or without a Safety Standards Certificate.

When the Buyer Agrees to Purchase

  • Confirm the final purchase price.

  • Confirm exactly what is included with the vehicle.

  • Confirm any known defects or problems with the buyer.

  • Receive and independently verify payment.

  • Complete the Bill of Sale.

  • Both buyer and seller sign and date the Bill of Sale.

  • Complete and sign the Application for Transfer on the Vehicle Permit.

  • Record the exact sale date.

  • Record the exact sale time for your records.

  • Give the buyer the Vehicle Permit's vehicle portion with the transfer completed.

  • Give the buyer the UVIP.

  • Give the buyer the Safety Standards Certificate if one is being provided.

Before the Vehicle Leaves

  • Remove your front licence plate.

  • Remove your rear licence plate.

  • Keep the plate portion of the Vehicle Permit.

  • Confirm the buyer has the documents they need.

  • Confirm the buyer understands that they must arrange their own insurance and registration.

  • Do not allow the buyer to leave using your licence plates.

  • Keep copies/photos of all signed documentation.

Immediately After the Sale

  • Photograph/scan the signed Bill of Sale.

  • Photograph/scan the completed transfer section.

  • Save the UVIP documentation.

  • Save proof of payment.

  • Save the Marketplace conversation/listing.

  • Notify your auto insurer that the vehicle has been sold.

  • Store your licence plates and plate portion of the permit securely.

One particularly important point for your situation

For the 2015 Hyundai Elantra with 262,584 km you mentioned previously, I would approach the transaction a little differently from selling a relatively new, low-mileage car.

I'd strongly consider advertising it as:

Private sale — sold as-is, where-is — Safety Standards Certificate not included

and make the listing unusually thorough about the car's mileage, known mechanical/cosmetic issues and history. That avoids spending potentially significant money making a 262,000+ km vehicle pass a safety inspection when a buyer may prefer to buy it at a lower price and decide themselves whether to repair it.

The key distinction is that "as-is" does not mean "I can hide problems." It means the buyer is purchasing the vehicle in its disclosed condition and is not receiving a warranty from you.

Also, don't confuse selling the car with transferring your plates: in Ontario, the car changes owners, while your plates remain yours. Ontario+1

The entire process in one line

Prepare car → get UVIP → advertise → meet buyer → test drive/inspection → agree on price → verify payment → sign Bill of Sale → complete permit transfer → give buyer UVIP/vehicle portion → remove your plates → buyer arranges insurance/registration → notify your insurer → retain your records.

The Ontario government specifically confirms that the seller must provide the UVIP, Bill of Sale and completed transfer documentation, while the buyer is responsible for registering the vehicle in their name. Ontario
